_comment: Which standard gamepad element drives each ares input, per console.
The left side is ares' own input name inside the block named by `layout`;
the right side is SDL's name for a standard element, which SDL maps to
whatever raw index a given controller actually uses. That indirection is
the point: the same table works for a pad whose A is button 0 and one whose
A is button 1.
A value may be a list. ares holds three bindings per input — an unbound one
reads `;;`, which is two separators around three empty slots — and any of
them drives it. That is how the analog stick doubles as the D-pad on the
consoles that never had one: both are bound, and either works.
An element ending in - or + is one direction of an analog axis: - is the
low side (up, or left), + the high side. Elements without a sign are
buttons, hats or triggers, whose direction is not in question.
ares' N64 Gamepad carries L-Up/L-Down/L-Left/L-Right beside X-Axis and
Y-Axis: they are the analog stick's digital corners, for a pad that has
no stick. They are deliberately left unbound. Bound to the D-pad -- which
they were -- the D-pad shoved the stick to full deflection as well as
sending a D-pad press, and the gate's own screen read `L-Up - D-pad up`
under `Up - D-pad up`, which is how it was noticed. Bound to the stick
instead they would be worse: the stick would saturate the moment it
crossed the threshold and DK64 would walk at one speed.
A name containing / is an input nested one level deeper, which is how ares
spells a true analog axis: `X-Axis/Lo` is the Lo line inside the X-Axis
block. Binding those is what makes a stick analog rather than four
switches.
`layout` is where the block lives. Consoles with controller ports nest
under Controller.Port.<n>; the handhelds have one built-in pad and nest
under their own name with no port number. Every name here — console,
container and pad alike — is read off a real settings.bml. ares writes a
console's section the first time that console runs, so none of them can be
guessed from the platform slug, and a wrong one would write bindings that
nothing ever reads.
